title: Roots That Make the Shortest Tree
statement:
You get an undirected tree with n nodes labelled 0 to n − 1, as a list of n − 1 edges. You may pick any node as the root. The height of the rooted tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Return every node that, as the root, gives the smallest possible height. The order of the returned labels does not matter.

examples.why: Rooted at 3 the farthest node is 5, two edges away. Rooted at 4 the farthest are 0, 1 and 2, also two edges away. Every other root gives height 3 or more. Picking only the node with the most neighbours would miss 4.
A path of four nodes has two middle nodes, each giving height 2.
A single node is its own best root, with height 0.

constraints: The edges form one tree with no repeated edges
hints: A leaf is never a good root when the tree has more than two nodes. Why?
Remove all current leaves at once. The best roots of the remaining tree are the same as before, because every height dropped by exactly 1.
Keep peeling leaf layers, like a topological sort on degrees, until at most two nodes are left. Those are the answer.

explain.intuition:
The height from a root is set by the longest path in the tree (its diameter): the best root sits in the middle of that path, and a path has either one middle node or two. So the answer always has one or two nodes.

To find the middle without computing the diameter, peel the tree like an onion. Every leaf is at the edge, so removing all leaves at once shortens every longest path by one at both ends and keeps the same middle. Repeat until one or two nodes remain. It is Kahn's topological sort, run on degree-1 nodes of an undirected tree.
steps: Build adjacency lists and the degree of every node. Put every node with degree 1 into the current layer.
While more than 2 nodes remain: remove the whole current layer, subtract it from remaining, and for every neighbour lower its degree; neighbours that reach degree 1 form the next layer.
pitfalls: Removing leaves one at a time instead of layer by layer. Then you can stop with the wrong pair of nodes.
Stopping when one node is left only. Two middle nodes are a valid answer and both must be returned.
Forgetting n = 1: there are no edges and no leaves, but node 0 is the answer.

solutions.title: BFS from every node
solutions.idea: Compute the height from each possible root with a BFS and keep the roots with the smallest height.

solutions.title: Peel leaf layers
solutions.idea: Strip all leaves at once, again and again. The last one or two nodes are the centre of the tree.

followups: Solve it with two BFS runs: find one end of the diameter, then the other end, then take the middle of that path.
Return the height of every possible root in O(n) total. (Hint: rerooting DP.)
